query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The controlled introduction of high-thermal-conductivity phases or reinforcements, specifically Al0.5CoCrFeNi2 high-entropy alloy (HEA) particles, into W–Cu metal-matrix composites will increase thermal conductivity by 15% while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance under heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint application conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu metal-matrix composites in their initial state with existing microstructure and properties
generation.intervention: Controlled introduction of 10 wt% Al0.5CoCrFeNi2 HEA particles
generation.conditions: Heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, with operating temperatures between 180–350 °C
generation.mechanism: The high-thermal-conductivity HEA particles will enhance the thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite by creating a conductive pathway for heat transfer, while the HEA's high entropy and sluggish diffusion effect will help retain mechanical durability and irradiation resistance
generation.baseline: Thermal conductivity of an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite without HEA particles
generation.uncertainty: The actual increase in thermal conductivity may vary depending on the specific processing conditions, microstructure, and interface bonding between the HEA particles and the W–Cu matrix

falsification_experiment.design: Measure the thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites with and without 10 wt% Al0.5CoCrFeNi2 HEA particles under heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint application conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite with HEA particles is not at least 10% higher than that of the composite without HEA particles, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed. Both (as-sintered) alloys were irradiated with Ar+ (150 keV) with a fluence of 2.4 × 1020 at/m2, as well as He+ (10 keV) and D+ (5 keV) both with a fluence of 5 × 1021 at/m2. Th

In this study, AZ91 magnesium-alloy-based metal matrix composites (MMCs) reinforced with 10 wt% of Al0.5CoCrFeNi2 high-entropy alloy (HEA) particles and SiC particles were prepared by a spark plasma sintering (SPS) process at 300 °C. The effects of reinforcements on the microstructure and mechanical properties of AZ91-based MMCs were studied. The results showed that AZ91–HEA composite consisted of α-Mg, Mg17Al12 and FCC phases. No interfacial reaction layer was observed between HEA particles and the Mg matrix. After adding HEA into AZ91, the compressive yield strength (C.Y.S) of the AZ91–HEA composite increased by 17% without degradation of failure strain. In addition, the increment in C.Y.S brought by HEA was comparable to that contributed by commonly used SiC reinforcement (15%). A relatively low porosity in the composite and enhanced interfacial bonding between the α-Mg matrix and HEA particles make HEA a potential reinforcement material in MMCs.

Recently, an emerging category of alloys, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has attracted lots of attention. Unlike conventional alloys, HEAs consist of five or more principal elements, and each element’s concentration is from 5 to 35 at% []. Because of the four essential effects, such as high-entropy effect, sluggish diffusion effect, severe lattice distortion and cocktail effect, HEAs possess high strength, excellent corrosion resistance and wear resistance. In addition to traditional structural applications, potential applications of HEAs can be found in surface coating, environmental protection, gas sensing, energy storage and waste heat recovery [,]. HEAs also have good wettability with metal and thermal expansion coefficients similar to those of metals. Thus, it has potential for the application as a reinforcement in Mg-alloy-based metal matrix composites and can solve the compatibility issue between metal matrices and ceramic reinforcements. HEAs can be classified into 3D transition metal HEAs, 4f transition metal HEAs, refractory metal HEAs and light metal HEAs [].
